1. Executive Overview

American Express (AXP) has delivered a cumulative total return of 24894.87% over more than five decades, translating to a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.81%. An investor who purchased shares at the adjusted closing price of $1.22 in June 1972 and held through March 2026 would see their position valued at $305.99 per share — a remarkable multi-decade wealth compounding outcome.

However, this journey was far from smooth. The stock endured a maximum drawdown of -83.91%, with the most severe episode occurring during the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, when AXP — as a major financial services company — was particularly exposed to credit and liquidity stress. Other notable drawdowns include the 1973–74 oil crisis, the dot-com bust, and the COVID-19 crash of 2020.

AXP has also been a consistent dividend payer, distributing a cumulative $34.27 per share in dividends over the dataset period. For income-focused investors, the stock has offered a reliable and growing dividend stream, particularly from the 1990s onward.

Key Takeaway: AXP's long-term track record demonstrates the power of compounding in a high-quality financial franchise, but investors must be prepared for periodic drawdowns of 40–70% during systemic financial crises.

2. Long-Term Price Trend Analysis

The logarithmic price chart below illustrates AXP's multi-decade trajectory. The log scale is essential for comparing percentage moves across eras — a $1 move in 1975 (when the stock traded under $2) is fundamentally different from a $1 move at $300+ in 2025. Shaded red bands mark the four most significant bear-market episodes.

Price with Moving Averages

The 50-day and 200-day moving averages provide a smoother view of the trend. Sustained periods where the 50-day MA trades above the 200-day MA ("golden cross") coincide with bull phases, while crossovers to the downside ("death cross") often precede extended drawdowns.

CAGR by Sub-Period

Breaking the full period into distinct eras reveals dramatically different growth rates. The 1980s and 1990s were AXP's strongest decades for price appreciation, while the 2000s — dominated by the dot-com crash and the Global Financial Crisis — produced a negative CAGR.

Bull & Bear Phase Summary

Major Bull Phases: 1982–1987 (financial deregulation), 1990–2000 (credit card boom), 2009–2020 (post-GFC recovery), 2020–2025 (post-COVID rebound).
Major Bear Phases: 1973–1974 (oil crisis, −74.69% peak drawdown), 2000–2002 (dot-com bust), 2007–2009 (GFC, worst drawdown on record), Feb–Mar 2020 (COVID-19 crash).

Decade Highlights:
• 1970s: A turbulent start — the oil crisis and stagflation produced deep drawdowns, but the decade ended with a recovery.
• 1980s: Financial deregulation and AXP's expansion drove strong price appreciation and moderate volatility.
• 1990s: The credit card boom era — AXP's strongest CAGR decade, benefiting from consumer credit growth.
• 2000s: The "lost decade" for AXP — the dot-com crash and GFC erased gains, producing a negative CAGR and the worst drawdown on record.
• 2010s: A steady recovery decade, with the GFC wounds healing and dividends resuming growth.
• 2020s: COVID-19 crash followed by a V-shaped recovery and continued strength through early 2026.
